claim: Latrophilin-2 (Lphn2) and latrophilin-3 (Lphn3) are adhesion GPCRs that serve as postsynaptic recognition molecules in CA1 pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus.
source: Latrophilin-2 (Lphn2) and latrophilin-3 (Lphn3) are adhesion GPCRs that serve as postsynaptic recognition molecules in CA1 pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus, where they are localized to distinct dendritic domains and are essential for different sets of excitatory synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019) as referenced in the Introduction section.

claim: Lphn2 and Lphn3 are localized to distinct dendritic domains in CA1 pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus.
source: Latrophilin-2 (Lphn2) and latrophilin-3 (Lphn3) are adhesion GPCRs that serve as postsynaptic recognition molecules in CA1 pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus, where they are localized to distinct dendritic domains and are essential for different sets of excitatory synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: Lphn2 and Lphn3 are essential for different sets of excitatory synapses in CA1 pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus.
source: Latrophilin-2 (Lphn2) and latrophilin-3 (Lphn3) are adhesion GPCRs that serve as postsynaptic recognition molecules in CA1 pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus, where they are localized to distinct dendritic domains and are essential for different sets of excitatory synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: Latrophilins are abundantly and differentially expressed in the cerebellar cortex.
source: We show that latrophilins are abundantly and differentially expressed in the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA-FISH data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The Lphn2/3 double-deletion suppresses parallel-fiber synapses.
source: Using conditional KO mice, we demonstrate that the Lphn2/3 double-deletion but not the deletion of Lphn2 or Lphn3 alone suppresses parallel-fiber synapses and reduces parallel-fiber synaptic transmission by ~50% without altering release probability.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4 and electrophysiology data in Figure 5.

claim: The deletion of Lphn2 alone does not suppress parallel-fiber synapses.
source: Using conditional KO mice, we demonstrate that the Lphn2/3 double-deletion but not the deletion of Lphn2 or Lphn3 alone suppresses parallel-fiber synapses and reduces parallel-fiber synaptic transmission by ~50% without altering release probability.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3A-D showing no significant changes in parallel-fiber synapses with Lphn2 deletion alone.

claim: The deletion of Lphn3 alone does not suppress parallel-fiber synapses.
source: Using conditional KO mice, we demonstrate that the Lphn2/3 double-deletion but not the deletion of Lphn2 or Lphn3 alone suppresses parallel-fiber synapses and reduces parallel-fiber synaptic transmission by ~50% without altering release probability.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3E-H showing no significant changes in parallel-fiber synapses with Lphn3 deletion alone.

claim: The Lphn2/3 double-deletion reduces parallel-fiber synaptic transmission by ~50%.
source: Using conditional KO mice, we demonstrate that the Lphn2/3 double-deletion but not the deletion of Lphn2 or Lphn3 alone suppresses parallel-fiber synapses and reduces parallel-fiber synaptic transmission by ~50% without altering release probability.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 5B showing reduced input-output relation and EPSC slope.

claim: The Lphn2/3 double-deletion does not alter release probability at parallel-fiber synapses.
source: Using conditional KO mice, we demonstrate that the Lphn2/3 double-deletion but not the deletion of Lphn2 or Lphn3 alone suppresses parallel-fiber synapses and reduces parallel-fiber synaptic transmission by ~50% without altering release probability.
evidence: This claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio data in Figure 5C showing no change in PPR.

claim: Climbing-fiber synapses were unaffected by the Lphn2/3 double-deletion.
source: Climbing-fiber synapses, conversely, were unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4B and electrophysiology data in Figure 5D.

claim: ~50% of total cerebellar Lphn3 protein is expressed in Bergmann glia.
source: Even though ~50% of total cerebellar Lphn3 protein is expressed in Bergmann glia, Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia did not detectably impair excitatory or inhibitory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2G showing ~50% reduction in Lphn3 levels after GLAST-Cre mediated deletion.

claim: Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia did not detectably impair excitatory synaptic transmission.
source: Even though ~50% of total cerebellar Lphn3 protein is expressed in Bergmann glia, Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia did not detectably impair excitatory or inhibitory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 7B-C showing no changes in excitatory synaptic transmission.

claim: Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia did not detectably impair inhibitory synaptic transmission.
source: Even though ~50% of total cerebellar Lphn3 protein is expressed in Bergmann glia, Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia did not detectably impair excitatory or inhibitory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 7D showing no changes in inhibitory synaptic transmission.

claim: Lphn2 and Lphn3 are selectively but redundantly required in Purkinje cells for parallel-fiber synapses.
source: Our studies demonstrate that Lphn2 and Lphn3 are selectively but redundantly required in Purkinje cells for parallel-fiber synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data showing that only double deletion, not single deletions, impairs parallel-fiber synapses (Figures 3-5).

claim: Brain function is thought to be mediated by information processing in neural circuits that are constructed via formation of synaptic connections between neurons.
source: Brain function is thought to be mediated by information processing in neural circuits that in turn are constructed via formation of synaptic connections between neurons.
evidence: This is a general statement about neuroscience based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Neural circuit wiring requires directed growth of axons towards target regions.
source: Neural circuit wiring requires directed growth of axons towards target regions, self-avoidance of axons and dendrites, axon-dendrite target selection, and formation and specification of synapses (Hassan and Hiesinger, 2015; Yogev and Shen, 2014; Zipursky and Sanes, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hassan and Hiesinger, 2015; Yogev and Shen, 2014; Zipursky and Sanes, 2010).

source: Neural circuit wiring requires directed growth of axons towards target regions, self-avoidance of axons and dendrites, axon-dendrite target selection, and formation and specification of synapses (Hassan and Hiesinger, 2015; Yogev and Shen, 2014; Zipursky and Sanes, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hassan and Hiesinger, 2015; Yogev and Shen, 2014; Zipursky and Sanes, 2010).

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hassan and Hiesinger, 2015; Yogev and Shen, 2014; Zipursky and Sanes, 2010).

claim: Much is known about axon guidance.
source: Although much is known about axon guidance, the molecular mechanisms governing target selection and synapse formation remain largely unclear.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The molecular mechanisms governing target selection and synapse formation remain largely unclear.

claim: Synaptic adhesion molecules form trans-synaptic complexes across the synaptic cleft.
source: Synaptic adhesion molecules form trans-synaptic complexes across the synaptic cleft that are thought to initiate synapse formation, maintain synapse stability, and regulate synapse properties (Südhof, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Südhof, 2018).

claim: Trans-synaptic complexes formed by synaptic adhesion molecules are thought to initiate synapse formation.
source: Synaptic adhesion molecules form trans-synaptic complexes across the synaptic cleft that are thought to initiate synapse formation, maintain synapse stability, and regulate synapse properties (Südhof, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Südhof, 2018).

claim: Trans-synaptic complexes formed by synaptic adhesion molecules are thought to maintain synapse stability.
source: Synaptic adhesion molecules form trans-synaptic complexes across the synaptic cleft that are thought to initiate synapse formation, maintain synapse stability, and regulate synapse properties (Südhof, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Südhof, 2018).

claim: Trans-synaptic complexes formed by synaptic adhesion molecules are thought to regulate synapse properties.
source: Synaptic adhesion molecules form trans-synaptic complexes across the synaptic cleft that are thought to initiate synapse formation, maintain synapse stability, and regulate synapse properties (Südhof, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Südhof, 2018).

claim: Latrophilins and BAIs may be unique because these adhesion GPCRs are among the few molecules whose deletion not only alters synaptic transmission, but actually decrease synapse numbers.
source: Many synaptic adhesion molecules have been identified, of which latrophilins and BAIs may be unique because these adhesion GPCRs are among the few molecules whose deletion not only alters synaptic transmission, but actually decrease synapse numbers, which suggests that these adhesion GPCRs are involved in synapse formation and maintenance (Bolliger et al., 2011; Kakegawa et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Bolliger et al., 2011; Kakegawa et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: The deletion of latrophilins and BAIs suggests that these adhesion GPCRs are involved in synapse formation and maintenance.
source: Many synaptic adhesion molecules have been identified, of which latrophilins and BAIs may be unique because these adhesion GPCRs are among the few molecules whose deletion not only alters synaptic transmission, but actually decrease synapse numbers, which suggests that these adhesion GPCRs are involved in synapse formation and maintenance (Bolliger et al., 2011; Kakegawa et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Bolliger et al., 2011; Kakegawa et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: The conditional deletion of latrophilin-2 (Lphn2) from CA1-region pyramidal neurons caused a selective loss of synapses formed in the Stratum lacunosum-moleculare by inputs from the entorhinal cortex.
source: In particular, we recently observed that the conditional deletion of latrophilin-2 (Lphn2) from CA1-region pyramidal neurons caused a selective loss of synapses formed in the Stratum lacunosum-moleculare by inputs from the entorhinal cortex, whereas the conditional deletion of latrophilin-3 (Lphn3) caused a selective loss of synapses formed in the Stratum oriens and Stratum radiatum by Schaffer-collateral inputs from the CA3 region (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: The conditional deletion of latrophilin-3 (Lphn3) from CA1-region pyramidal neurons caused a selective loss of synapses formed in the Stratum oriens and Stratum radiatum by Schaffer-collateral inputs from the CA3 region.
source: In particular, we recently observed that the conditional deletion of latrophilin-2 (Lphn2) from CA1-region pyramidal neurons caused a selective loss of synapses formed in the Stratum lacunosum-moleculare by inputs from the entorhinal cortex, whereas the conditional deletion of latrophilin-3 (Lphn3) caused a selective loss of synapses formed in the Stratum oriens and Stratum radiatum by Schaffer-collateral inputs from the CA3 region (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: Rescue experiments involving overexpression of Lphn2 or Lphn3 revealed that Lphn2 and Lphn3 were non-redundant in the CA1-region.
source: Importantly, rescue experiments involving overexpression of Lphn2 or Lphn3 revealed that Lphn2 and Lphn3 were non-redundant in the CA1-region (Sando et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sando et al., 2019).

claim: Lphn2 and Lphn3 could only rescue the phenotype of the deletion of the eponymous gene, but not of the deletion of the other gene in CA1-region neurons.
source: These two adhesion GPCRs could only rescue the phenotype of the deletion of the eponymous gene, but not of the deletion of the other gene, demonstrating an unexpected functional diversification of highly homologous genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sando et al., 2019).

claim: The rescue experiments demonstrate an unexpected functional diversification of highly homologous genes.
source: These two adhesion GPCRs could only rescue the phenotype of the deletion of the eponymous gene, but not of the deletion of the other gene, demonstrating an unexpected functional diversification of highly homologous genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sando et al., 2019) and represents an inference from the rescue experiment results.

claim: Latrophilins function as postsynaptic adhesion molecules.
source: These results not only demonstrated that latrophilins function as postsynaptic adhesion molecules, but also that they exhibit synapse specificity and are essential for the existence of their target synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: Latrophilins exhibit synapse specificity.
source: These results not only demonstrated that latrophilins function as postsynaptic adhesion molecules, but also that they exhibit synapse specificity and are essential for the existence of their target synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: Latrophilins are essential for the existence of their target synapses.
source: These results not only demonstrated that latrophilins function as postsynaptic adhesion molecules, but also that they exhibit synapse specificity and are essential for the existence of their target synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: The three latrophilin genes are differentially expressed in cerebellum, but in overlapping patterns.
source: Single molecule RNA fluorescent in situ hybridizations (smRNA-FISH) showed that the three latrophilin genes are differentially expressed in cerebellum, but in overlapping patterns (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 1.

claim: All latrophilins are expressed in cerebellar cortex.
source: All latrophilins are expressed in cerebellar cortex; in addition, Lphn1, Lphn2 and to a lesser extent Lphn3 are expressed in deep cerebellar nuclei (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Lphn1, Lphn2 and to a lesser extent Lphn3 are expressed in deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: All latrophilins are expressed in cerebellar cortex; in addition, Lphn1, Lphn2 and to a lesser extent Lphn3 are expressed in deep cerebellar nuclei (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the cerebellar cortex, Lphn1 is primarily expressed in granule cells.
source: In the cerebellar cortex, Lphn1 is primarily expressed in granule cells, Lphn2 in Purkinje cells, and Lphn3 in Bergmann glia (that are also localized to the Purkinje cell layer) and in interneurons (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: In the cerebellar cortex, Lphn2 is primarily expressed in Purkinje cells.
source: In the cerebellar cortex, Lphn1 is primarily expressed in granule cells, Lphn2 in Purkinje cells, and Lphn3 in Bergmann glia (that are also localized to the Purkinje cell layer) and in interneurons (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: In the cerebellar cortex, Lphn3 is primarily expressed in Bergmann glia and in interneurons.
source: In the cerebellar cortex, Lphn1 is primarily expressed in granule cells, Lphn2 in Purkinje cells, and Lphn3 in Bergmann glia (that are also localized to the Purkinje cell layer) and in interneurons (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Transcripts for all Lphn isoforms are found in Purkinje cells.
source: Quantification of Lphn RNA puncta in Purkinje cell bodies revealed that transcripts for all Lphn isoforms are found in Purkinje cells and that Lphn1 and Lphn2 puncta were more abundant than Lphn3 puncta (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lphn1 and Lphn2 puncta were more abundant than Lphn3 puncta in Purkinje cells.
source: Quantification of Lphn RNA puncta in Purkinje cell bodies revealed that transcripts for all Lphn isoforms are found in Purkinje cells and that Lphn1 and Lphn2 puncta were more abundant than Lphn3 puncta (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nestin-Cre nearly completely ablated Lphn2 and Lphn3 expression.
source: Nestin-Cre nearly completely ablated Lphn2 and Lphn3 expression as expected (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: L7-Cre had no significant effect on the levels of either Lphn2 or Lphn3.
source: L7-Cre had no significant effect on the levels of either Lphn2 or Lphn3, although there was a trend towards a decrease for Lphn2 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There was a trend towards a decrease for Lphn2 with L7-Cre.
source: L7-Cre had no significant effect on the levels of either Lphn2 or Lphn3, although there was a trend towards a decrease for Lphn2 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The number of Purkinje cells is much lower than that of other cerebellar neurons.
source: However, despite their remarkable size and prominence, the number of Purkinje cells is much lower than that of other cerebellar neurons (e.g., granule cells, interneurons, and deep cerebellar nuclei neurons), and the selective loss of Lphn2 and Lphn3 from Purkinje cells may have been occluded by the combined levels of these proteins in other neurons, in particular granule cells and deep cerebellar nuclei neurons.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy.

claim: The selective loss of Lphn2 and Lphn3 from Purkinje cells may have been occluded by the combined levels of these proteins in other neurons.
source: However, despite their remarkable size and prominence, the number of Purkinje cells is much lower than that of other cerebellar neurons (e.g., granule cells, interneurons, and deep cerebellar nuclei neurons), and the selective loss of Lphn2 and Lphn3 from Purkinje cells may have been occluded by the combined levels of these proteins in other neurons, in particular granule cells and deep cerebellar nuclei neurons.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the lack of detectable change in Figure 2D.

claim: Both Lphn2 and Lphn3 were significantly decreased in PV-Cre mice.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, both Lphn2 and Lphn3 were significantly decreased in PV-Cre mice that express Cre in deep cerebellar nuclei neurons and interneurons in addition to Purkinje cells, with Lphn2 expression reduced by nearly 80% (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Lphn2 expression was reduced by nearly 80% in PV-Cre mice.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, both Lphn2 and Lphn3 were significantly decreased in PV-Cre mice that express Cre in deep cerebellar nuclei neurons and interneurons in addition to Purkinje cells, with Lphn2 expression reduced by nearly 80% (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Math-Cre had no significant effect on the levels of Lphn2 and Lphn3.
source: Math-Cre, conversely, had no significant effect on the levels of Lphn2 and Lphn3, consistent with the fact that granule cells primarily express Lphn1 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Granule cells primarily express Lphn1.
source: Math-Cre, conversely, had no significant effect on the levels of Lphn2 and Lphn3, consistent with the fact that granule cells primarily express Lphn1 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA-FISH data in Figure 1 and immunoblot data in Figure 2F.

claim: GLAST-Cre-mediated deletion of Lphn2 and Lphn3 in Bergmann glia did not detectably alter the levels of Lphn2.
source: GLAST-Cre-mediated deletion of Lphn2 and Lphn3 in Bergmann glia, finally, did not detectably alter the levels of Lphn2, but dramatically decreased the levels of Lphn3, indicative of substantial Lphn3 expression in these astrocytes (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: GLAST-Cre-mediated deletion of Lphn2 and Lphn3 in Bergmann glia dramatically decreased the levels of Lphn3.
source: GLAST-Cre-mediated deletion of Lphn2 and Lphn3 in Bergmann glia, finally, did not detectably alter the levels of Lphn2, but dramatically decreased the levels of Lphn3, indicative of substantial Lphn3 expression in these astrocytes (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The dramatic decrease in Lphn3 levels with GLAST-Cre is indicative of substantial Lphn3 expression in Bergmann glia.
source: GLAST-Cre-mediated deletion of Lphn2 and Lphn3 in Bergmann glia, finally, did not detectably alter the levels of Lphn2, but dramatically decreased the levels of Lphn3, indicative of substantial Lphn3 expression in these astrocytes (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an inference from the immunoblot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Latrophilins are postsynaptic adhesion molecules.
source: Since latrophilins are postsynaptic adhesion molecules and Purkinje cells are the postsynaptic target of almost all synapses in the cerebellar cortex, we focused our analyses of the cerebellar role of latrophilins on Purkinje cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: Purkinje cells are the postsynaptic target of almost all synapses in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Since latrophilins are postsynaptic adhesion molecules and Purkinje cells are the postsynaptic target of almost all synapses in the cerebellar cortex, we focused our analyses of the cerebellar role of latrophilins on Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy.

claim: No significant difference in vGluT1 staining intensity was observed between sections from control mice and mice lacking either Lphn2 or Lphn3 in the Purkinje cells.
source: We observed no significant difference in vGluT1 staining intensity between sections from control mice and mice lacking either Lphn2 or Lphn3 in the Purkinje cells (Figure 3A and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A and E.

claim: No difference in input resistance and capacitance of Purkinje cells was detected between control and Lphn2- or Lphn3-deficient Purkinje cells.
source: Next, we cut acute slices from the mice and used whole-cell patch-clamp recordings to measure the input resistance and capacitance of Purkinje cells, but again detected no difference between control and Lphn2- or Lphn3-deficient Purkinje cells (Figure 3B and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3B and F.

claim: No differences in paired-pulse ratio of EPSCs were observed between Purkinje cells expressing or lacking Lphn2 or Lphn3.
source: Finally, we monitored parallel-fiber EPSCs induced by extracellular stimulation in the upper molecular layer, and determined both the paired-pulse ratio of EPSCs in response to two stimuli separated by 50 ms and the overall synaptic strength quantified by the input-output relation and the rise slope of EPSCs (Figure 3C–D and G–H). Here, we also observed no differences between Purkinje cells expressing or lacking Lphn2 or Lphn3, suggesting that each isoform alone is not essential for proper parallel-fiber synapse numbers or parallel-fiber synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3C and G.

claim: No differences in overall synaptic strength were observed between Purkinje cells expressing or lacking Lphn2 or Lphn3.
source: Finally, we monitored parallel-fiber EPSCs induced by extracellular stimulation in the upper molecular layer, and determined both the paired-pulse ratio of EPSCs in response to two stimuli separated by 50 ms and the overall synaptic strength quantified by the input-output relation and the rise slope of EPSCs (Figure 3C–D and G–H). Here, we also observed no differences between Purkinje cells expressing or lacking Lphn2 or Lphn3, suggesting that each isoform alone is not essential for proper parallel-fiber synapse numbers or parallel-fiber synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3D and H.

claim: Each isoform alone is not essential for proper parallel-fiber synapse numbers or parallel-fiber synaptic transmission.
source: Finally, we monitored parallel-fiber EPSCs induced by extracellular stimulation in the upper molecular layer, and determined both the paired-pulse ratio of EPSCs in response to two stimuli separated by 50 ms and the overall synaptic strength quantified by the input-output relation and the rise slope of EPSCs (Figure 3C–D and G–H). Here, we also observed no differences between Purkinje cells expressing or lacking Lphn2 or Lphn3, suggesting that each isoform alone is not essential for proper parallel-fiber synapse numbers or parallel-fiber synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is an inference from the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lphn2/3 double-deficient sections displayed a ~ 30% decrease in vGluT1 staining intensity.
source: Strikingly, we found that the Lphn2/3 double-deficient sections displayed a ~ 30% decrease in vGluT1 staining intensity, suggesting a decrease in parallel-fiber synapses (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ~ 30% decrease in vGluT1 staining intensity suggests a decrease in parallel-fiber synapses.
source: Strikingly, we found that the Lphn2/3 double-deficient sections displayed a ~ 30% decrease in vGluT1 staining intensity, suggesting a decrease in parallel-fiber synapses (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference from the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The density of vGluT2-positive puncta was unchanged by the Lphn2/3 double deletion.
source: The density of vGluT2-positive puncta and of vGAT-positive puncta was unchanged (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The density of vGAT-positive puncta was unchanged by the Lphn2/3 double deletion.
source: The density of vGluT2-positive puncta and of vGAT-positive puncta was unchanged (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Parallel fibers form synapses onto secondary and tertiary dendrites.
source: The two types of excitatory inputs onto Purkinje cells can be distinguished anatomically as parallel fibers form synapses onto secondary and tertiary dendrites while climbing-fibers form synapses onto primary dendrites that are closer to the Purkinje cell soma.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy.

claim: Climbing-fibers form synapses onto primary dendrites that are closer to the Purkinje cell soma.
source: The two types of excitatory inputs onto Purkinje cells can be distinguished anatomically as parallel fibers form synapses onto secondary and tertiary dendrites while climbing-fibers form synapses onto primary dendrites that are closer to the Purkinje cell soma.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy.

claim: Homer1 puncta density was reduced on distal tertiary dendrites but not primary dendrites of Purkinje cells in Lphn2/3 double-deficient sections.
source: In support of a reduction of parallel-fiber but not climbing-fiber synapse number, we stained Lphn2/3 double-deficient sections for Homer1 and found that Homer1 puncta density was reduced on distal tertiary dendrites but not primary dendrites of Purkinje cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No difference in synaptic protein levels was found in cerebellar lysates from control and Lphn2/3 double-KO mice.
source: In addition, we compared synaptic protein levels of cerebellar lysates from control and Lphn2/3 double-KO mice by immunoblot and found no difference in any of the proteins tested, including vGluT1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A reduction in vGluT1 levels at Purkinje cell synapses in the cerebellar cortex may be obscured by abundant vGluT1 expression in other regions of the cerebellum.
source: As discussed in our immunoblot analysis with the L7-Cre line in Figure 2D,a reduction in vGluT1 levels at Purkinje cell synapses in the cerebellar cortex may be obscured by abundant vGluT1 expression in other regions of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the lack of detectable change in vGluT1 levels by immunoblot.

claim: The double Lphn2/3 deletion may specifically alter parallel-fiber synapses.
source: Overall, these results indicate that the double Lphn2/3 deletion may specifically alter parallel-fiber synapses, suggesting a redundant function of Lphn2 and Lphn3 in these synapses.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4.

claim: Lphn2 and Lphn3 have a redundant function in parallel-fiber synapses.
source: Overall, these results indicate that the double Lphn2/3 deletion may specifically alter parallel-fiber synapses, suggesting a redundant function of Lphn2 and Lphn3 in these synapses.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined data showing that only double deletion, not single deletions, impairs parallel-fiber synapses.

claim: Lphn2/3-deficient and control Purkinje cells exhibited the same capacitance and input resistance values.
source: Lphn2/3-deficient and control Purkinje cells exhibited the same capacitance and input resistance values, suggesting that the double deletion did not grossly impair the development of Purkinje cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The double deletion did not grossly impair the development of Purkinje cells.
source: Lphn2/3-deficient and control Purkinje cells exhibited the same capacitance and input resistance values, suggesting that the double deletion did not grossly impair the development of Purkinje cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an inference from the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Input-output measurements of parallel-fiber synaptic responses uncovered an approximately 50% decrease in parallel-fiber synaptic strength.
source: Input-output measurements of parallel-fiber synaptic responses, however, uncovered an approximately 50% decrease in parallel-fiber synaptic strength, confirming the immunohistochemistry findings that suggest that parallel-fiber synapses are impaired by the double Lphn2/3 deletion (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The approximately 50% decrease in parallel-fiber synaptic strength confirms the immunohistochemistry findings that suggest that parallel-fiber synapses are impaired by the double Lphn2/3 deletion.
source: Input-output measurements of parallel-fiber synaptic responses, however, uncovered an approximately 50% decrease in parallel-fiber synaptic strength, confirming the immunohistochemistry findings that suggest that parallel-fiber synapses are impaired by the double Lphn2/3 deletion (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the electrophysiology data in Figure 5B with the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4.

claim: The decrease in parallel-fiber synaptic strength is likely not due to a decrease in release probability.
source: This decrease is likely not due to a decrease in release probability, as demonstrated by a lack of change in paired-pulse ratios (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an inference from the paired-pulse ratio data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The amplitude of climbing-fiber EPSCs was normal in Lphn2/3 double-deficient Purkinje cells.
source: Analyses of climbing-fiber synaptic responses showed that the amplitude, paired-pulse ratio, and step number of climbing-fiber EPSCs (reflecting the number of climbing fibers innervating a Purkinje cell) were normal in Lphn2/3 double-deficient Purkinje cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio of climbing-fiber EPSCs was normal in Lphn2/3 double-deficient Purkinje cells.
source: Analyses of climbing-fiber synaptic responses showed that the amplitude, paired-pulse ratio, and step number of climbing-fiber EPSCs (reflecting the number of climbing fibers innervating a Purkinje cell) were normal in Lphn2/3 double-deficient Purkinje cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The step number of climbing-fiber EPSCs was normal in Lphn2/3 double-deficient Purkinje cells.
source: Analyses of climbing-fiber synaptic responses showed that the amplitude, paired-pulse ratio, and step number of climbing-fiber EPSCs (reflecting the number of climbing fibers innervating a Purkinje cell) were normal in Lphn2/3 double-deficient Purkinje cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The step number of climbing-fiber EPSCs reflects the number of climbing fibers innervating a Purkinje cell.
source: Analyses of climbing-fiber synaptic responses showed that the amplitude, paired-pulse ratio, and step number of climbing-fiber EPSCs (reflecting the number of climbing fibers innervating a Purkinje cell) were normal in Lphn2/3 double-deficient Purkinje cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about climbing-fiber electrophysiology.

claim: No differences in the average mEPSC frequency were observed between Lphn2/3 double-deficient and control Purkinje cells.
source: Recordings of spontaneous mEPSCs performed in the presence of tetrodotoxin revealed no differences in the average mEPSC frequency between Lphn2/3 double-deficient and control Purkinje cells (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: The majority of mEPSCs with 10–90% rise times of less than 0.6 ms are derived from climbing fibers that are insensitive to Group III mGluR agonists.
source: The majority of mEPSCs with 10–90% rise times of less than 0.6 ms are derived from climbing fibers that are insensitive to Group III mGluR agonists, while the majority of mEPSCs with 10–90% rise times greater than 2 ms are derived from parallel-fiber synapses that are severely depressed in response to Group III mGluR agonists (Ichikawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ichikawa et al., 2016).

claim: The majority of mEPSCs with 10–90% rise times greater than 2 ms are derived from parallel-fiber synapses that are severely depressed in response to Group III mGluR agonists.
source: The majority of mEPSCs with 10–90% rise times of less than 0.6 ms are derived from climbing fibers that are insensitive to Group III mGluR agonists, while the majority of mEPSCs with 10–90% rise times greater than 2 ms are derived from parallel-fiber synapses that are severely depressed in response to Group III mGluR agonists (Ichikawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ichikawa et al., 2016).

claim: The frequency of mEPSCs with rise times less than 0.6 ms was unchanged between Lphn2/3 double cKO and control cells.
source: The frequency of mEPSCs with rise times less than 0.6 ms was unchanged between Lphn2/3 double cKO and control cells, whereas the frequency of mEPSCs with rise times greater than 2 ms was reduced by ~25%, a difference that was almost statistically significant (p=0.07).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The frequency of mEPSCs with rise times greater than 2 ms was reduced by ~25% in Lphn2/3 double cKO cells.
source: The frequency of mEPSCs with rise times less than 0.6 ms was unchanged between Lphn2/3 double cKO and control cells, whereas the frequency of mEPSCs with rise times greater than 2 ms was reduced by ~25%, a difference that was almost statistically significant (p=0.07).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The reduction in frequency of mEPSCs with rise times greater than 2 ms was almost statistically significant (p=0.07).
source: The frequency of mEPSCs with rise times less than 0.6 ms was unchanged between Lphn2/3 double cKO and control cells, whereas the frequency of mEPSCs with rise times greater than 2 ms was reduced by ~25%, a difference that was almost statistically significant (p=0.07).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: A significant difference in the cumulative frequency distribution of mEPSC amplitudes was observed despite minimal difference in average mEPSC amplitude after the Lphn2/3 deletion.
source: A significant difference in the cumulative frequency distribution of mEPSC amplitudes was observed despite minimal difference in average mEPSC amplitude after the Lphn2/3 deletion (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The average 10–90% rise times of mEPSCs was significantly reduced in Lphn2/3 deficient Purkinje cells compared to control.
source: The average 10–90% rise times of mEPSCs was significantly reduced in Lphn2/3 deficient Purkinje cells compared to control, however, the average rise times for both the <0.6 ms and >2 ms subgroups of mEPSCs were unchanged, suggesting that the reduction in average mEPSC rise time was the result of the altered proportion of parallel-fiber to climbing-fiber events after Lphn2/3 double KO rather than a change in intrinsic mEPSC properties of either synaptic input (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The average rise times for both the <0.6 ms and >2 ms subgroups of mEPSCs were unchanged in Lphn2/3 deficient Purkinje cells.
source: The average 10–90% rise times of mEPSCs was significantly reduced in Lphn2/3 deficient Purkinje cells compared to control, however, the average rise times for both the <0.6 ms and >2 ms subgroups of mEPSCs were unchanged, suggesting that the reduction in average mEPSC rise time was the result of the altered proportion of parallel-fiber to climbing-fiber events after Lphn2/3 double KO rather than a change in intrinsic mEPSC properties of either synaptic input (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The reduction in average mEPSC rise time was the result of the altered proportion of parallel-fiber to climbing-fiber events after Lphn2/3 double KO rather than a change in intrinsic mEPSC properties of either synaptic input.
source: The average 10–90% rise times of mEPSCs was significantly reduced in Lphn2/3 deficient Purkinje cells compared to control, however, the average rise times for both the <0.6 ms and >2 ms subgroups of mEPSCs were unchanged, suggesting that the reduction in average mEPSC rise time was the result of the altered proportion of parallel-fiber to climbing-fiber events after Lphn2/3 double KO rather than a change in intrinsic mEPSC properties of either synaptic input (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is an inference from the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: No changes in mIPSC amplitude or frequency were observed between control and Lphn2/3-deficient Purkinje cells.
source: Recordings of spontaneous miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) revealed no changes in mIPSC amplitude or frequency between control and Lphn2/3-deficient Purkinje cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The double deletion of both Lphn2 and Lphn3, as opposed to the single deletion of each latrophilin isoform individually, causes a selective and robust impairment of parallel-fiber synapses.
source: Overall, these data indicate that the double deletion of both Lphn2 and Lphn3, as opposed to the single deletion of each latrophilin isoform individually, causes a selective and robust impairment of parallel-fiber synapses.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the combined data in Figures 3-5.

claim: The selective high-level expression of Lphn3 in Bergmann glia in the cerebellum is consistent with single-cell RNAseq data.
source: Given the selective high-level expression of Lphn3 in Bergmann glia in the cerebellum we observed by in situ hybridization analyses (Figures 1 and 2) that is consistent with single-cell RNAseq data (Saunders et al., 2018; Zeisel et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014; Koirala and Corfas, 2010), we asked whether Lphn3 might have a synaptic organizing function in these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Saunders et al., 2018; Zeisel et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014; Koirala and Corfas, 2010).

claim: The expression of neuroligin-3 in Bergmann glia appears to be essential for the function of parallel-fiber synapses.
source: This question was prompted by our unpublished finding that the expression of neuroligin-3, another postsynaptic adhesion molecule, in Bergmann glia appears to be essential for the function of parallel-fiber synapses (Zhang, B. and Südhof, T.C., submitted).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to unpublished work (Zhang, B. and Südhof, T.C., submitted).

claim: Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia caused a major decrease in Lphn3 protein levels in total cerebellum.
source: Thus, we used Lphn3 cKO mice crossed with GLAST-CreER mice to delete Lphn3 from astrocytic Bergmann glia in the cerebellum, employing daily 4-OHT injections from age P10-P12 to induce Cre recombination (Figure 6A). This manipulation caused a major decrease in Lphn3 protein levels as determined by immunoblot in total cerebellum (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: A similar decrease in Lphn3 staining intensity was observed in the cerebellar cortex after deletion of Lphn3 in Bergmann glia.
source: Consistent with this observation, we observed a similar decrease in Lphn3 staining intensity (visualized by the HA-epitope knock-in) in the cerebellar cortex after deletion of Lphn3 in Bergmann glia (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The majority of Lphn3 in cerebellar cortex is expressed by Bergmann glia.
source: These results indicate that the majority of Lphn3 in cerebellar cortex is expressed by Bergmann glia, and that despite the functional importance of Lphn3 in Purkinje cells as described above, the Lphn3 levels in Purkinje cells are much lower than those in Bergmann glia.
evidence: This is an inference from the immunoblot and immunohistochemistry data in Figures 2G and 6B.

claim: Despite the functional importance of Lphn3 in Purkinje cells, the Lphn3 levels in Purkinje cells are much lower than those in Bergmann glia.
source: These results indicate that the majority of Lphn3 in cerebellar cortex is expressed by Bergmann glia, and that despite the functional importance of Lphn3 in Purkinje cells as described above, the Lphn3 levels in Purkinje cells are much lower than those in Bergmann glia.
evidence: This is an inference from the immunoblot and immunohistochemistry data in Figures 2G and 6B.

claim: The deletion of Lphn3 from Bergmann glia had no effect on vGluT1 staining intensity.
source: As above, we quantified parallel-fiber synapses by overall vGluT1 staining intensity because the density of parallel-fiber synapses is too high to enable resolution of individual puncta by confocal microscopy. The resulting vGluT1 staining intensity reflects a combination of parallel-fiber synapse density and size (Zhang et al., 2015). The deletion of Lphn3 from Bergmann glia had no effect on this parameter (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: vGluT1 staining intensity reflects a combination of parallel-fiber synapse density and size.
source: As above, we quantified parallel-fiber synapses by overall vGluT1 staining intensity because the density of parallel-fiber synapses is too high to enable resolution of individual puncta by confocal microscopy. The resulting vGluT1 staining intensity reflects a combination of parallel-fiber synapse density and size (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: No change in climbing-fiber density was observed after Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia.
source: We then quantified the density, staining intensity, and size of vGluT2-positive puncta that represent climbing-fiber synapses. We observed no change in climbing-fiber density, but a significant decrease in their staining intensity and size, hinting at a possible impairment (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A significant decrease in climbing-fiber staining intensity and size was observed after Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia.
source: We then quantified the density, staining intensity, and size of vGluT2-positive puncta that represent climbing-fiber synapses. We observed no change in climbing-fiber density, but a significant decrease in their staining intensity and size, hinting at a possible impairment (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The decrease in climbing-fiber staining intensity and size hints at a possible impairment.
source: We then quantified the density, staining intensity, and size of vGluT2-positive puncta that represent climbing-fiber synapses. We observed no change in climbing-fiber density, but a significant decrease in their staining intensity and size, hinting at a possible impairment (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is speculation based on the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: No significant changes in inhibitory synapses were observed after Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia.
source: Moreover, we investigated inhibitory synapses both in the upper molecular and the Purkinje cell layer that are presumably derived from stellate cells and basket cells, respectively, but again observed no significant changes (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The staining pattern intensity for GLAST, GLT-1, and GluA1 were indistinguishable between sections from control mice and mice in which Lphn3 had been deleted from Bergmann glia postnatally.
source: We used immunocytochemistry to stain the cerebellar cortex of littermate-control homozygous Lphn3 cKO mice containing or lacking a GLAST-Cre allele for three Bergmann glia-specific markers: the glutamate transporters GLAST and GLT-1, and the glutamate receptor GluA1 (Figure 6F; Rothstein et al., 1994; Bergles et al., 1997; Saab et al., 2012). For every glial marker, the staining pattern intensity were indistinguishable between sections from control mice and mice in which Lphn3 had been deleted from Bergmann glia postnatally, suggesting that Bergmann glia were unaffected by Lphn3 deletion (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Bergmann glia were unaffected by Lphn3 deletion.
source: We used immunocytochemistry to stain the cerebellar cortex of littermate-control homozygous Lphn3 cKO mice containing or lacking a GLAST-Cre allele for three Bergmann glia-specific markers: the glutamate transporters GLAST and GLT-1, and the glutamate receptor GluA1 (Figure 6F; Rothstein et al., 1994; Bergles et al., 1997; Saab et al., 2012). For every glial marker, the staining pattern intensity were indistinguishable between sections from control mice and mice in which Lphn3 had been deleted from Bergmann glia postnatally, suggesting that Bergmann glia were unaffected by Lphn3 deletion (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is an inference from the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: No changes in any synaptic protein were observed after Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia, except for a decrease in the levels of vGAT and a trend towards a decrease for CASK and gephyrin.
source: To independently confirm this conclusion, we analyzed the cerebellum from control mice and mice with a deletion of Lphn3 from Bergmann glia by quantitative immunoblotting for a series of synaptic marker proteins (Figure 6G). We observed no changes in any synaptic protein, in particular not in vGluT1 and vGluT2 that are specific for parallel-fiber and climbing-fiber synapses, respectively, except for a decrease in the levels of vGAT that is specific for inhibitory synapses, and a trend towards a decrease for the scaffolding proteins CASK and gephyrin.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The deletion of Lphn3 from Bergmann glia does not cause a major change in the structure and composition of the cerebellar cortex.
source: These results confirm that the deletion of Lphn3 from Bergmann glia, the major cell type in cerebellum in which Lphn3 is expressed, does not cause a major change in the structure and composition of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined immunohistochemistry and immunoblot data in Figure 6.

claim: The Lphn3 deletion in Bergmann glia has no major effect on the basic properties of Purkinje cells.
source: Using whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from Purkinje cells in acute cerebellar slices, we confirmed by measurements of the capacitance and input resistance that the Lphn3 deletion in Bergmann glia has no major effect on the basic properties of Purkinje cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Evoked climbing-fiber synaptic responses were unchanged in either amplitude, paired-pulse ratio or number of 'steps' after Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia.
source: Evoked climbing-fiber synaptic responses were unchanged in either amplitude, paired-pulse ratio or number of 'steps' (reflecting the number of climbing fibers innervating a Purkinje cell) after Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The frequency and amplitude of mEPSCs were unchanged after Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia.
source: Measurements of spontaneous miniature EPSCs and IPSCs (performed in the presence of tetrodotoxin) showed that the frequency and amplitude of mEPSCs and of mIPSCs were also unchanged (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The frequency and amplitude of mIPSCs were unchanged after Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia.
source: Measurements of spontaneous miniature EPSCs and IPSCs (performed in the presence of tetrodotoxin) showed that the frequency and amplitude of mEPSCs and of mIPSCs were also unchanged (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Despite high levels of Lphn3 expression in Bergmann glia, Lphn3 is not essential in this type of astrocyte for any of the major synaptic components of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Thus, despite high levels of Lphn3 expression in Bergmann glia, Lphn3 is not essential in this type of astrocyte for any of the major synaptic components of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Unlike the function of Lphn2 and Lphn3 in hippocampal CA1-region neurons, Lphn2 and Lphn3 perform redundant functions in Purkinje cells.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that unlike the function of Lphn2 and Lphn3 in hippocampal CA1-region neurons, Lphn2 and Lphn3 perform redundant functions in Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined data showing that only double deletion, not single deletions, impairs parallel-fiber synapses in Purkinje cells.

claim: Lphn2 and Lphn3 function selectively targets parallel-fiber synapses in Purkinje cells.
source: This function selectively targets parallel-fiber synapses, corroborating the synapse specificity observed in hippocampus.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The synapse specificity of Lphn2 and Lphn3 in Purkinje cells corroborates the synapse specificity observed in hippocampus.
source: This function selectively targets parallel-fiber synapses, corroborating the synapse specificity observed in hippocampus.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings with prior work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: The effect of the Lphn2/3 double deletion on Purkinje cells is selective for parallel-fiber synapses.
source: The effect of the Lphn2/3 double deletion on Purkinje cells is selective for parallel-fiber synapses as evidenced by immunocytochemistry for specific synaptic markers (Figure 4) and by electrophysiological recordings of evoked and spontaneous synaptic transmission (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference from the combined data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The most parsimonious explanation for the impairment of parallel-fiber synapses in Lphn2/3-deficient Purkinje cells is that there is a decrease in synapse numbers.
source: The most parsimonious explanation for the impairment of parallel-fiber synapses in Lphn2/3-deficient Purkinje cells is that there is a decrease in synapse numbers because the vGluT1 staining intensity in the cerebellar cortex was decreased and the strength of parallel-fiber synapses was suppressed without a change in paired-pulse ratio.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The Lphn2/3 double deletion phenotype resembles that of the Lphn2 and Lphn3 single deletions in CA1-region neurons of the hippocampus.
source: In this respect, the Lphn2/3 double deletion phenotype resembles that of the Lphn2 and Lphn3 single deletions in CA1-region neurons of the hippocampus in which we also observed a loss of synapses without a change in release probability that was restricted to specific subset of excitatory synapses (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings with prior work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: The L7 promoter used for Purkinje cell-specific Cre recombination initiates Cre expression at P9-10.
source: The L7 promoter used for Purkinje cell-specific Cre recombination initiates Cre expression at P9-10, which is during the period of parallel-fiber synaptogenesis (Barski et al., 2000; Mishina et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Barski et al., 2000; Mishina et al., 2012).

claim: P9-10 is during the period of parallel-fiber synaptogenesis.
source: The L7 promoter used for Purkinje cell-specific Cre recombination initiates Cre expression at P9-10, which is during the period of parallel-fiber synaptogenesis (Barski et al., 2000; Mishina et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Barski et al., 2000; Mishina et al., 2012).

claim: Excitatory synaptic transmission onto CA1 neurons of the hippocampus is similarly impaired by Lphn3 deletion at P0 and P21.
source: While the current study does not distinguish between a role for Lphns in synapse formation versus synapse maintenance, excitatory synaptic transmission onto CA1 neurons of the hippocampus is similarly impaired by Lphn3 deletion at P0 and P21, suggesting that Lphns may have a broad role in excitatory synapse maintenance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sando et al., 2019).

claim: Lphns may have a broad role in excitatory synapse maintenance.
source: While the current study does not distinguish between a role for Lphns in synapse formation versus synapse maintenance, excitatory synaptic transmission onto CA1 neurons of the hippocampus is similarly impaired by Lphn3 deletion at P0 and P21, suggesting that Lphns may have a broad role in excitatory synapse maintenance.
evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings and prior work (Sando et al., 2019).

claim: Many synaptic adhesion molecules, including neurexins and neuroligins, are expressed in glia.
source: Many synaptic adhesion molecules, including neurexins and neuroligins, are expressed in glia (Saunders et al., 2018; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Saunders et al., 2018; Zeisel et al., 2018).

claim: The Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia caused a ~ 50% decrease in cerebellar Lphn3 protein content.
source: Our quantitative immunoblotting and smRNA-FISH data show that Lphn3 is expressed in Bergmann glia at extraordinarily high levels, as evidenced by the fact that the Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia caused a ~ 50% decrease in cerebellar Lphn3 protein content (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Deletion of latrophilin-3 from Bergmann glia had no major effect on Bergmann glia markers or synaptic parameters in the cerebellum.
source: Nevertheless, deletion of latrophilin-3 from Bergmann glia had no major effect on Bergmann glia markers or synaptic parameters in the cerebellum (Figures 6–7).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: A small decrease in climbing-fiber synapse puncta size and intensity was observed by immunohistochemistry after Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia.
source: Although we observed a small decrease in climbing-fiber synapse puncta size and intensity by immunohistochemistry, climbing-fiber synaptic transmission was unchanged, suggesting that Lphn3 expression in Bergmann glia is not essential for the fundamental properties of these cerebellar synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Climbing-fiber synaptic transmission was unchanged after Lphn3 deletion from Bergmann glia.
source: Although we observed a small decrease in climbing-fiber synapse puncta size and intensity by immunohistochemistry, climbing-fiber synaptic transmission was unchanged, suggesting that Lphn3 expression in Bergmann glia is not essential for the fundamental properties of these cerebellar synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Lphn3 expression in Bergmann glia is not essential for the fundamental properties of cerebellar synapses.
source: Although we observed a small decrease in climbing-fiber synapse puncta size and intensity by immunohistochemistry, climbing-fiber synaptic transmission was unchanged, suggesting that Lphn3 expression in Bergmann glia is not essential for the fundamental properties of these cerebellar synapses.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The lack of a phenotype in Bergmann glia is unexpected when comparing the effect of the Lphn3 deletion in Purkinje cells to that in Bergmann glia.
source: This lack of a phenotype is unexpected especially if one compares the effect of the Lphn3 deletion when induced in combination with the Lphn2 deletion in Purkinje cells in the analyses of the Lphn2/3 double-deficient condition to that of the Lphn3 deletion in Bergmann glia.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the results in Purkinje cells versus Bergmann glia.

claim: In Purkinje cells, Lphn3 is barely detectable by in situ hybridization.
source: In Purkinje cells, Lphn3 is barely detectable by in situ hybridization and the deletion of Lphn3 from Purkinje cells has no significant effect on the overall cerebellar Lphn3 content; nevertheless, its deletion from Purkinje cells causes a massive impairment in parallel-fiber synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The deletion of Lphn3 from Purkinje cells has no significant effect on the overall cerebellar Lphn3 content.
source: In Purkinje cells, Lphn3 is barely detectable by in situ hybridization and the deletion of Lphn3 from Purkinje cells has no significant effect on the overall cerebellar Lphn3 content; nevertheless, its deletion from Purkinje cells causes a massive impairment in parallel-fiber synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Deletion of Lphn3 from Purkinje cells causes a massive impairment in parallel-fiber synapses.
source: In Purkinje cells, Lphn3 is barely detectable by in situ hybridization and the deletion of Lphn3 from Purkinje cells has no significant effect on the overall cerebellar Lphn3 content; nevertheless, its deletion from Purkinje cells causes a massive impairment in parallel-fiber synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: In Bergmann glia, Lphn3 levels are so high that they contribute ~50% to the total cerebellar Lphn3 content.
source: In Bergmann glia, in contrast, Lphn3 levels are so high that they contribute ~50% to the total cerebellar Lphn3 content even with widespread Lphn3 expression elsewhere in cerebellum, but here deletion of Lphn3 is without major consequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Deletion of Lphn3 from Bergmann glia is without major consequences.
source: In Bergmann glia, in contrast, Lphn3 levels are so high that they contribute ~50% to the total cerebellar Lphn3 content even with widespread Lphn3 expression elsewhere in cerebellum, but here deletion of Lphn3 is without major consequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The expression levels of a protein are not necessarily indicative of its functional importance in a given cell type.
source: This example illustrates again a conclusion that has previously been proposed many times, namely that the expression levels of a protein are not necessarily indicative of its functional importance in a given cell type.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of Lphn3 function in Purkinje cells versus Bergmann glia.

claim: The phenotype of the Lphn2 and Lphn3 deletions is similar in magnitude to that of the cerebellin-1 deletion.
source: Finally, one may ask why the phenotype of the Lphn2 and Lphn3 deletions, although very significant and similar in magnitude to that of the cerebellin-1 deletion (Ito-Ishida et al., 2008), is not even stronger at parallel-fiber synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ito-Ishida et al., 2008).

claim: There may be further redundancy between Lphn1 with Lphn2 and Lphn3.
source: It seems likely that there may be further redundancy between Lphn1, the latrophilin isoform that was not examined here, with Lphn2 and Lphn3.
evidence: This is speculation about potential redundancy with Lphn1.

claim: Lphn1 is highly expressed in many cerebellar cell types.
source: Lphn1 is highly expressed in many cerebellar cell types (Figure 1), but no cKO mice are currently available.
evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 1.

claim: No cKO mice for Lphn1 are currently available.
source: Lphn1 is highly expressed in many cerebellar cell types (Figure 1), but no cKO mice are currently available.
evidence: This is a statement about the availability of research tools.

claim: Lphn1 may be redundant with Lphn2 and Lphn3.
source: Given the redundancy between Lphn2 and Lphn3 observed here, presumably Lphn1 may also be redundant with Lphn2 and Lphn3, and a triple Lphn1/2/3 deletion could potentially have a much bigger impact on synaptic function than a double deletion of Lphn2 and Lphn3.
evidence: This is speculation about potential redundancy with Lphn1.

claim: A triple Lphn1/2/3 deletion could potentially have a much bigger impact on synaptic function than a double deletion of Lphn2 and Lphn3.
source: Given the redundancy between Lphn2 and Lphn3 observed here, presumably Lphn1 may also be redundant with Lphn2 and Lphn3, and a triple Lphn1/2/3 deletion could potentially have a much bigger impact on synaptic function than a double deletion of Lphn2 and Lphn3.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential effect of a triple deletion.

claim: The results reveal a selective redundant function of Lphn2 and Lphn3 as postsynaptic adhesion molecules in parallel-fiber synapses of the cerebellum.
source: In summary, our results reveal a selective redundant function of Lphn2 and Lphn3 as postsynaptic adhesion molecules in parallel-fiber synapses of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the combined data in Figures 3-5.

claim: The results extend the previous conclusion obtained in hippocampal CA1 region neurons that Lphn2 and Lphn3 are essential postsynaptic adhesion molecules.
source: These results extend the previous conclusion obtained in hippocampal CA1 region neurons that Lphn2 and Lphn3 are essential postsynaptic adhesion molecules, but demonstrate that although Lphn2 and Lphn3 perform distinct functions in these hippocampal neurons, they perform redundant functions in Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings with prior work (Anderson et al., 2017; Sando et al., 2019).

claim: Although Lphn2 and Lphn3 perform distinct functions in hippocampal neurons, they perform redundant functions in Purkinje cells.
source: These results extend the previous conclusion obtained in hippocampal CA1 region neurons that Lphn2 and Lphn3 are essential postsynaptic adhesion molecules, but demonstrate that although Lphn2 and Lphn3 perform distinct functions in these hippocampal neurons, they perform redundant functions in Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined data showing different patterns of redundancy in hippocampus versus cerebellum.
